title: When inventions kill!
summary: Josh and Chuck cover people who died by their own inventions or experiments: Henry Winstanley (Eddystone Lighthouse collapse), Marie Curie (radiation poisoning, mentioned briefly), Harry Daghlian (Demon core criticality accident), and then the "official five": Li Si (Qin dynasty legalist minister executed by the "five pains"/ling chi), Franz Reichelt (failed parachute suit jump from the Eiffel Tower, 1912), Max Valier (rocket engine explosion, rocket car and rocket sled pioneer), William Bullock (rotary printing press inventor killed by his press in 1867), and Michael Dacre (JetPod air taxi crash in 2009). Episode ends with listener mail from Scott Miller about how animal color blindness is tested using operant conditioning.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode premise
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with brief banter about the Kavanaugh hearing, then introduce the episode theme of people who died by their own inventions.

segments.title: Early examples: Winstanley, Curie, Daghlian
segments.summary: Hosts recount Henry Winstanley's death when the Eddystone Lighthouse collapsed in a storm, note Marie Curie's radiation poisoning, and describe Harry Daghlian's Demon core accident in which a dropped tungsten carbide brick caused a criticality incident, leading to his death within a month.

segments.title: Li Si and the five pains
segments.summary: Hosts describe Li Si, a clerk who rose to prime minister under the Qin dynasty, his legalist governance, book burning, and his alleged invention of the five pains execution. After the emperor's death he helped forge a decree that led to a son's suicide, and was later executed by Zhao Gao's rival Zhao... (Joo Chow) through the five pains, said to resemble ling chi slow slicing.

segments.title: Franz Reichelt and the Eiffel Tower parachute
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the history of early parachute development in France, including Lenormand, who coined the term parachute, and Franz Reichelt, a tailor whose flying suit failed when he jumped from the Eiffel Tower in front of newsreel cameras after a dummy test from his apartment window.

segments.title: Max Valier and rocket cars
segments.summary: Max Valier, a self-taught amateur engineer inspired by Hermann Oberth's book, developed rocket cars and rocket sleds with Opel, then died in May 1930 when a rocket motor exploded and a shard of shrapnel severed his aorta. The hosts also mention the Verein fur Raumschiffahrt and Arthur Rudolph's later work on Saturn V.

segments.title: William Bullock and the rotary printing press
segments.summary: Hosts trace printing press history from flat presses to Richard Hoe's cylinder press, then to William Bullock's rotary web press. Bullock died in 1867 when his leg was caught in the rollers of a press he was repairing while it was running at the Philadelphia Public Ledger; the leg became gangrenous and he died after amputation surgery.

segments.title: Michael Dacre and the JetPod
segments.summary: Hosts describe British pilot Michael Dacre's JetPod very quiet short takeoff and landing aircraft concept as an air taxi linking Heathrow and central London. He died in 2009 during a test flight in Malaysia when the prototype failed to get airborne on several attempts and then rose vertically and crashed.

segments.title: Listener mail: animal color blindness testing
segments.summary: Scott Miller explains how researchers test color blindness in animals using operant conditioning, where animals press levers for treats only when a specific color is shown.
